opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's one of the most interesting puzzles in interpretability right now. The short answer is that networks seem to exploit sparsity.

Start with representation, which is the better-understood half. The idea of superposition is that a network can represent more features than it has dimensions. In a high-dimensional space you can fit far more vectors that are *almost* orthogonal than ones that are exactly orthogonal, exponentially many as dimensionality grows. If most features are inactive on any given input, which is true of the world (any one sentence is about only a tiny fraction of all possible concepts), then the network can pack many features into overlapping directions and pay only a small interference cost. When two features rarely co-occur, the crosstalk between them rarely matters, and nonlinearities can filter out a lot of the small noise.

The more interesting question, and the one you're getting at, is computation in superposition. It's not just storing more things than you have neurons, it's *doing* more operations than you have neurons. There's theoretical work showing that, in principle, you can implement many more logical operations, things like ANDs of pairs of features, than you have neurons, again as long as only a small number of those computations need to be active on any one input. Each neuron participates in many different little circuits, and each circuit is spread across many neurons. On a given forward pass most circuits are effectively off, so the ones that are on can borrow shared machinery without stepping on each other too badly.

That has big implications for how we try to understand these systems. If computation is happening in superposition, then the neuron is the wrong unit of analysis. A single neuron is polysemantic because it's a shared resource. That's why a lot of my recent work has shifted toward decomposing the *parameters* of the network rather than just the activations. Methods like attribution-based parameter decomposition, and the follow-up work on stochastic parameter decomposition, try to break the weights into a set of components where only a few are needed on any given input, but together they add up to the original network. The bet is that those components correspond to the actual mechanisms the network is running. If we can find them, we get a description of the network's computation that's faithful to how it actually works, rather than one forced to fit the neuron basis.

So the summary is: there's a lot more room in high-dimensional space than our intuitions suggest, the world is sparse, and gradient descent seems to find ways to exploit both. Our job as interpretability researchers is to find the right basis to untangle it.

r001.rationale: It says each neuron participates in many circuits and each circuit is spread across many neurons, enabling more logical operations than neurons.

r002.rationale: It explains that only a small number of computations are active on a given input and that inactive circuits are effectively off, allowing active circuits to share machinery.

r003.rationale: It explicitly extends superposition from representing more features than dimensions to performing more computations than neurons.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is the superposition story, and I think it's one of the most important ideas in interpretability right now. The basic observation is that if you think of each neuron as representing one feature, then a network with, say, ten thousand neurons in a layer should only be able to represent ten thousand things. But empirically that's clearly not what's happening. Language models seem to track vastly more concepts than they have neurons in any given layer.

The way they get around this is by not representing features along individual neurons at all. Instead, features get represented as directions in activation space, and crucially, those directions don't have to be orthogonal to one another. In a high-dimensional space you can pack in far more nearly-orthogonal directions than you have dimensions. The Johnson-Lindenstrauss intuition is roughly that the number of almost-orthogonal vectors you can fit grows exponentially with dimension. So the network trades a bit of interference between features for a huge increase in how many it can store.

The reason this works at all is sparsity. Most features aren't active at the same time. If you're reading a sentence about cooking, the features for medieval history or Python syntax are probably off. So the interference from overlapping directions only really bites when two features that share some overlap happen to co-occur, and if that's rare enough, the network can tolerate it. Anthropic's toy models paper made this quite concrete: you can watch a small model go from representing only the most important features cleanly to cramming many more in as you make the data sparser.

Where I think it gets more interesting, and this is closer to what I've been thinking about, is that this isn't just about storing features. It's also about computation. If you can superpose representations, you can plausibly superpose the operations on them too. A single weight matrix might be implementing many different little circuits at once, each operating on its own sparse subset of features, and they only step on each other's toes when the inputs collide. So the network isn't just a bigger lookup table than its neuron count suggests. It's running more distinct computations than you'd naively think it has capacity for.

And that raises the question I find most pressing for interpretability, which is: what's the right unit of analysis? If neurons aren't the right unit for representations, they're probably not the right unit for computation either. Sparse dictionary learning has given us a reasonable handle on the representation side, but the mechanism side, actually decomposing the weights or the computation into the pieces that are superposed, is much less solved. That's the frontier I'm most excited about.

r001.rationale: It says a single weight matrix can implement many circuits at once, each operating on its own sparse subset of features, extending distributed representations to computation.

r002.rationale: It explains that most features are inactive at a given time and that sparse activity limits interference, allowing many features and their computations to coexist.

r003.rationale: It explicitly describes superposing operations as an extension of superposed representations into computation.

astra-6.text:
Well, the key is that a neuron doesn’t have to correspond to just one feature or one computation. You can represent information in patterns of activity spread across many neurons, and those patterns can overlap. That’s the basic idea of superposition.

Imagine a space with a thousand dimensions. You can fit much more than a thousand directions into that space if you don’t require them all to be perfectly perpendicular. You get some interference between them, but if the features are sparse—if only a few are active on any particular input—that interference can be manageable.

The interesting question is then how you actually compute with those representations. Packing lots of features into a network isn’t, by itself, the same as performing lots of computations. But the idea is that the same neurons and weights can participate in different computations depending on which features are active. So counting neurons doesn’t necessarily tell you how many distinct computational operations the network has learned to carry out.

r001.rationale: It says information is represented in patterns spread across neurons and that the same neurons and weights can participate in different computations.

r002.rationale: It mentions sparse activity and manageable interference, but does not state that suppressing computations that should be inactive enables more computations to coexist.

r003.rationale: It describes representational superposition and conditional reuse of neurons for computations, but does not characterize overlapping distributed computations as an extension of superposition into computational space.

sol-6.1.text:
The key idea is that a neuron doesn’t have to correspond to just one feature or one computation. You can represent things as patterns of activity across many neurons, and those patterns can overlap. This is what people mean by superposition.

Imagine a high-dimensional space. You can fit many more directions into that space than you have dimensions, provided you’re willing to tolerate a little interference between them. If the features you care about are sparse—so only a small fraction are active on any particular input—that interference can be manageable.

Then the question is whether you can also do useful computation on those overlapping representations. And you can, at least in some settings: the same weights and neurons can participate in different computations depending on which features are active. So counting neurons doesn’t necessarily tell you how many distinct computations a network can carry out. The harder question is understanding which computations can share that machinery, and what happens when they interfere.

r001.rationale: It explains that features are represented by overlapping patterns across many neurons and that the same neurons can participate in different computations.

r002.rationale: It says sparse activity can make interference manageable, but does not state that suppressing computations that should be inactive enables more computations to coexist.

r003.rationale: It describes superposition of overlapping representations and then explains that useful computations can operate on those same overlapping representations.
